title: Cauda equina syndrome
summary: A sensitive red-flag history with a clear emergency plan.

domains.domain: Introduction, consent, privacy and chaperone offer
Bowel and sexual function, asked sensitively
PMH, drugs, allergies, social and work

aim.text: Assess a sensitive, focused history in a patient with back pain and possible cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency where speed protects bladder, bowel and sexual function.

items: Open with an open question, then use focused closed questions.
Ask about saddle numbness, bladder, bowel and sexual function, sensitively and in private.
Cover leg symptoms and other red flags.
Explain the urgency in plain language and state a plan: urgent MRI and early spinal team involvement.

candidateInstructions.text: You are the emergency department doctor. Mr Daniel Reid, 42, has come to the department with back pain. Observations are normal. Take a focused history. Do not examine. At the end, summarise and state your initial plan.

actorBriefs.title: Actor brief: patient, Mr Daniel Reid

blocks.text: Manner: worried, a little embarrassed about bladder and bowel questions.

After an open question: "I hurt my back lifting boxes five days ago. Now it's down both legs, and I'm struggling to pass water." After "anything else?": "My right foot keeps catching, and I feel numb in a weird place."

items: Back pain from lifting five days ago. Pain down both legs for two days, right worse. Right foot catching, no falls.
Since yesterday: numb around the back passage and inner thighs, can't feel toilet paper properly.
Bladder: hard to start, does not feel when full, dribbled this morning.
Bowels: constipated, did not feel the stool pass. Erections harder since yesterday (only if asked sensitively).
No fever, weight loss, cancer, IV drug use, recent infection or procedure, steroids or blood thinners. Only the lifting injury.
PMH: earlier back pain episodes, nothing serious. Takes ibuprofen and codeine. No allergies. Smokes 10 a day. Warehouse worker, lives with his partner.
Concerns (if asked): "Will I be paralysed? Will I work again? I can't cope with being incontinent."

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr Shah, one of the emergency doctors. Can you confirm your full name and date of birth?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Daniel Reid, 12th June 1984.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you. I'll need to ask some personal questions about your bladder and bowels. Are you comfortable here, or would you like more privacy or a chaperone?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Here is fine.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Could you tell me what has been happening, in your own words?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: I hurt my back lifting boxes five days ago. Now it's down both legs, and I'm struggling to pass water.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Thank you. Is there anything else you've noticed?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: My right foot keeps catching, and I feel numb in a weird place.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: I'm going to ask some specific questions now. Where exactly is the numbness? Is it around your back passage, genitals or inner thighs, the area that would touch a saddle?
Key finding: saddle numbness since yesterday.

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Yes, since yesterday. When I wipe, I can't feel it properly.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Is it hard to start passing urine? Can you feel when your bladder is full? Any leaking?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Hard to start, I don't feel it's full, and I dribbled this morning.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: What about your bowels?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Constipated, and I didn't feel it when I went.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: This next question is sensitive, but important. Any change in erections or sexual function?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Yes, harder since yesterday.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Is the leg pain in one leg or both? Any weakness, numbness or falls?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Both, the right is worse. My foot catches. No falls.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Any fever, weight loss, history of cancer, injecting drugs, recent infection or procedure, steroids or blood thinners?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: None of those.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Have you had back problems before? What medicines do you take? Any allergies? What do you do for work, and who is at home?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Some back aches before, nothing serious. Ibuprofen and codeine, no allergies. I work in a warehouse and live with my partner. I smoke ten a day.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: What is worrying you most?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Will I be paralysed? Will I work again? I can't cope with being incontinent.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Those are understandable worries. This is why we are acting quickly, because treating pressure on the nerves early gives the best chance of recovery.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.text: Let me summarise. Daniel, you hurt your back five days ago, and now have pain down both legs, a right foot that catches, numbness around your back passage, trouble passing urine, reduced bowel sensation and a change in sexual function. I'm worried this could be pressure on the bundle of nerves at the bottom of the spine, called cauda equina syndrome. It is an emergency. I'm arranging a bladder scan and an urgent MRI of your spine, and calling the spinal team now. I'll also examine you, including checking feeling and muscle tone around the back passage, with a chaperone. Is that alright?

lines.speaker: Patient
lines.text: Yes. Thank you.

head: Task
Expected in this station
rows: Do
Introduce yourself, check name and date of birth, offer privacy and a chaperone, start with an open question, ask sensitive questions kindly, signpost, summarise, state a plan.
Find

Five days of back pain after lifting, now bilateral leg pain (right worse), right foot catching, saddle numbness since yesterday, hesitancy and reduced bladder sensation, reduced bowel sensation, new sexual dysfunction, no other red flags.
Ask
Saddle sensation, bladder, bowel and sexual function, leg weakness, fever, cancer, injecting drug use, trauma, steroids, blood thinners, previous back problems, work and home, worries.
Manage
Say aloud: urgent senior and spinal team review, examination with chaperone including anal tone, bladder scan, emergency MRI spine, bloods, analgesia, baseline neurology, nil by mouth.
React
Acknowledge embarrassment and fear, stay calm, do not falsely reassure, say you would ask the senior when unsure.

head: Situation
Good response
rows: Patient is embarrassed
Pause, normalise the questions, offer privacy again, then continue.
Patient asks to go home
Explain the risk clearly, say you want him to stay for urgent scans, involve the senior.
Leg weakness gets worse
Tell the spinal team now, repeat the neurological check, note the time.
Patient cannot feel his bladder
Arrange a bladder scan without delay.
Time running out
Go straight to red flags and the summary with a plan.
Unsure of an examiner question
Say what you know, name the limit, and say you would ask a senior.

head: Medical term
Say instead
rows: Cauda equina
The bundle of nerves at the bottom of the spinal canal
Saddle anaesthesia
Numbness around the back passage, genitals and inner thighs, where a saddle would touch
Urinary retention
Not being able to empty your bladder
Radiculopathy
Nerve pain shooting down the leg
Foot drop
Your foot catching or dragging
MRI
A detailed scan with a magnet, no radiation
Bladder scan
A painless scan to see how much urine is in the bladder
Catheter
A thin tube to drain the bladder
Decompression
An operation to take pressure off the nerves
Erectile dysfunction
Changes in erections or sexual function

head: Question
Model reply
rows: Will I be paralysed?
"I cannot promise, but this is exactly why we are acting so fast. Relieving pressure on the nerves early gives the best chance."
Will my bladder recover?
"It depends on how long the nerves have been squeezed and how quickly we relieve it. That is why speed matters."
Do I need an operation?
"Possibly. The scan will show. If a disc is pressing on the nerves, urgent surgery is often needed."
Can I go home with painkillers?
"I am worried about you, so I want you to stay for an urgent scan and the spinal team."
Why the back passage examination?
"It checks the nerves there. A chaperone will be present, and you can ask me to stop at any time."
Will I work again?
"Let us focus on treatment first. We will talk about recovery and work afterwards."

patientQuestions.text: Tips: acknowledge the feeling first, short sentences, check understanding, no false reassurance.

examinerQuestions.question: What are your immediate actions and investigations?

items: Recognise a surgical emergency and escalate early to the senior and the on-call spinal or neurosurgical team.
Examine: leg power, tone, reflexes, sensation, saddle sensation, and with a chaperone anal tone and sensation.
Bladder scan for post-void residual volume.
Emergency MRI of the spine.
Bloods, analgesia, document a baseline neurological state, repeat observations, nil by mouth in case of surgery.
Large central lumbar disc prolapse (most common).
Spinal stenosis.
Tumour or metastases.
Epidural abscess or haematoma.
Trauma or fracture.

examinerQuestions.question: Which back pain red flags need urgent action?

items: Saddle numbness, new bladder or bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, bilateral or progressive leg weakness: emergency.
Also needing prompt work-up: cancer history, fever, injecting drug use, steroids, trauma, age under 20 or over 50, weight loss, night pain.

examinerQuestions.question: What is the difference between incomplete and retention types?

items: Incomplete: altered urinary sensation or stream, may still pass urine.
Retention: painless urinary retention with overflow, with a worse outlook.
Both are urgent. The aim is to decompress before retention develops.
Recovery of bladder, bowel and sexual function depends on how early pressure is relieved.
Delay risks permanent deficits, so MRI and surgery should happen as soon as possible, following the local spinal pathway.

Reassuring and discharging on painkillers.
